Under the cue, civilian casualties are primary for 12 models and success for 8; nine models switch from success to civilian casualties, and none switch in the opposite direction.53:T629,The paper proposes a framework, not a new metric. It starts by defining a taxonomy of behavioral correctness assumptions, then operationalizes each assumption through controlled response transformations. The assumptions are split into two groups.

1. Correctness-preserving assumptions: transformations that should not change correctness with respect to the reference, such as paraphrasing, stylistic variation, or equivalent reformulation. A reliable evaluator should assign similar scores before and after the transformation.
2. Correctness-altering assumptions: transformations that should reduce response quality, such as removing relevant information, adding factual errors, introducing logical inconsistency, or injecting irrelevant content. A reliable evaluator should lower the score accordingly.

Two design choices matter. First, the transformations are intended to isolate one property at a time, so score changes are attributable rather than confounded. Second, the framework is evaluator-agnostic: it can probe lexical, character-level, semantic, LLM-based, and hybrid evaluators under the same behavioral test suite. In that sense, the work is closer to a stress-testing methodology than to a leaderboard.

The paper also studies repeat-run variability, evaluator configuration sensitivity, and test-suite reproducibility. These are especially important for LLM judges, whose outputs can vary with prompts, decoding settings, or model versions. An evaluator that looks good on aggregate but is unstable across runs or configurations is risky as a training signal.54:T445,The empirical study covers a broad range of reference-based evaluators, including lexical overlap methods, character-level methods, semantic similarity methods, LLM-based evaluators, and hybrid systems. The main result is not that one family dominates everywhere, but that assumption-level analysis reveals distinct behavioral profiles that aggregate benchmark scores often hide. Lexical methods tend to be brittle under surface-form changes and therefore violate some correctness-preserving assumptions. Semantic and LLM-based methods are usually more robust to paraphrase, but may be less sensitive to certain correctness-altering transformations or more variable under configuration changes.

The paper also reports stability analyses across repeated runs, evaluator settings, and independently generated test suites. The key takeaway is that the proposed diagnostic framework itself appears reproducible enough to support meaningful evaluator characterization. For practical use, the most informative results are likely the per-assumption breakdowns rather than any averaged summary score.55:T5b8,The method has three layers. First, formalization: the benchmark score is written as a composition of stage-specific functions rather than a static dataset-plus-metric object. Second, auditing: under a common framework, the authors inspect eight benchmark implementations and identify 15 recurring failure modes, including prompt formatting, stop sequences, token budgets, handling of reasoning spans, output parsing, label aliases, binary versus partial-credit scoring, invalid-response treatment, and aggregation. Importantly, they do not stop at anecdotal examples. They run controlled perturbations, changing one pipeline field at a time while holding the rest fixed, and measure the effect on scores and rankings. Third, standardization: they build a harness that exposes and standardizes nine configuration fields wherever task semantics allow, so that differences caused by benchmark-specific evaluator choices can be separated from differences caused by the task itself. That has three useful implications. First, data organization can be more important than raw volume for sparse capabilities. First, capability decomposition. The authors define three levels: Level I for single-view spatial perception, Level II for cross-view scene understanding, and Level III for complex contextual spatial reasoning. The key point is not difficulty ranking but dependency: Level III tasks are constructed so they require the lower-level capabilities and cannot be solved through single-view shortcuts. Second, top-down data generation. Using 3D-grounded assets and multi-view scene sources, the pipeline starts from complex Level III tasks and then decomposes them into prerequisite Level I and II sub-questions. This is important because the lower-level questions are not sampled independently; they are generated as supporting steps for a coherent spatial cognition problem group. The ordered answers to these sub-questions naturally become chain-of-thought annotations. Third, capability-aligned training. From the available text, the training recipe appears to use the hierarchy in a staged way, spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, with the goal of keeping model reasoning aligned with the dependency structure encoded in the dataset. Compared with standard spatial benchmarks, the novelty is the coupling of task hierarchy, supervision structure, and training progression.59:T7fb,方法上，作者提出一个 estimand-aware 的 pairwise decision procedure。流程可以概括成四步。第一，明确比较对象和目标量：比较的是哪两个具体 configuration，分数估计的是 observed benchmark mix、equal-repository weighting、expert-labeled success、cost-aware utility，还是 deployment-like success rule。第二，检查 common support，也就是在目标重加权或分层后，两边是否都覆盖相同的 support cells；如果某些 repository、task cell、mode 或 label source 只在一边出现，就不能支持该目标下的公平比较。第三，在有支持的前提下估计 pairwise gap，并显式声明 uncertainty rule 和 practical margin。这里作者强调，不仅要给区间，还要说明不确定性是按 item、task cluster 还是更高层级来算，以及多重比较时是否用 simultaneous interval。第四，根据证据给 pairwise label，而不是强行输出全序排名。标签包括：stable superiority、target-sensitive、verifier disagreement、insufficient precision、missing support 等。

论文还做了三类补充设计。其一是 controlled checks：用模拟数据检验这些 decision labels 在有限样本下能否恢复已知真值。其二是已知 target 下的估计实验，验证在 common support 内做标准化和重加权时，若不把 uncertainty 纳入判断，会高估 target reweighting 导致“翻盘”的频率。其三是 AgentRewardBench 上的 permutation analysis，给出 task-conditioned exchangeability 参考，帮助理解在固定任务条件下 close gap 有多容易由采样波动产生。

和常见 leaderboard 分析不同，这篇文章不满足于“多报几个 metric”。作者的关键区分是：多 metric 只有在每个 metric 的 estimand 都被说清时才有意义。raw success rate 只是 observed mix 下的量，不等于 equal-weighted repo success，也不等于 expert-verified success，更不等于 cost-adjusted utility。这个区分是全文最重要的技术立场。5a:T7a7,实验部分的价值主要在于把“close ranks 不可靠”说得很具体，而不是停留在原则层面。文中给出的几个结果很关键。

1. SWE-bench Verified：作者考察公开 raw top-10 之间形成的 45 个 pair。在 descriptive pointwise 95% interval 加上 2-point decision rule 下，只有 5 个比较可判为 stable，1 个是 target-sensitive，39 个属于 underpowered。若改用更严格的 max-deviation simultaneous interval，45 个 pair 一个都无法判定。这说明 close rank difference 在 item 数有限、pair 数多时，几乎不支持强 pairwise superiority 结论。

2. AgentRewardBench：同一批 agent 用不同 label source 会改写榜首。expert labels 选出 Claude 3.7 Sonnet 为第一，而 GPT-4o-mini judge labels 则选 GPT-4o 为第一。作者把这类现象归为 verifier disagreement：不是 agent 本身一定变了，而是 measurement source 变了，估计的量也随之改变。对依赖 LLM judge 的评测，这一点尤其重要。

3. tau2-bench：协议和成本规则会改变结论。文中指出，在可比 primary runs 上，pass@4 相比 pass@1 会把分数抬高 17.7 到 20.4 个点；而一旦把 cost 纳入 utility rule，被选中的系统也可能变化。也就是说，重复尝试规则和预算约束不是“展示细节”，而是 estimand 的一部分。

4. 粗粒度公开记录的限制：对 DataAgentBench 和 Open Agent，作者说明如果没有 item-level uncertainty 或细粒度日志，能做的只剩 score reweighting 和 grouped comparison，很多 pairwise claim 根本无法识别。这一点对 benchmark 发布规范有现实意义。

整体上，实验没有追求复杂模型，而是用公开日志、重加权、区间估计、置换检验和有限样本分析，证明 close comparisons 更多是“无法判定”，而不是“稳定翻转”。这个结论比简单说“leaderboard 不可靠”更细，也更有操作性。5b:T6f0,The central contribution is an estimand-aware pairwise decision procedure. It has four parts. First, define the comparison target explicitly: which two configurations are being compared, and what quantity is the score intended to estimate—raw success on the observed benchmark mix, equal-repository weighting, expert-labeled success, deployment-style success, or cost-aware utility. Second, check common support under that target. If the two systems do not both cover the same support cells after stratification or reweighting, the target comparison is not identified from the released data. Third, estimate the supported gap and attach a stated uncertainty rule plus a practical margin. The paper stresses that uncertainty is not a cosmetic add-on: one must specify the sampling unit, clustering level, and whether simultaneous inference is needed. Fourth, return a decision label rather than forcing a total order. Labels include stable superiority, target-sensitive, verifier disagreement, insufficient precision, and missing support.

The paper also includes controlled checks. Simulations test whether these labels recover known finite-sample states. A known-target estimation exercise shows why target reweighting must be judged with uncertainty included; otherwise one overstates how often rankings “flip.” An AgentRewardBench permutation analysis provides a task-conditioned exchangeability reference for interpreting close gaps.

What distinguishes this from routine leaderboard commentary is the insistence that multiple metrics help only if each metric’s estimand is explicit. Raw success, equal-weighted success, expert-verified success, and cost-adjusted utility are different quantities. Treating them as interchangeable is the source of many overclaims.5c:T64d,The empirical section is useful because it turns a general warning into concrete failure modes.

1. SWE-bench Verified: among the 45 pairs formed from the observed raw top 10, a descriptive pointwise 95% interval with a 2-point decision rule yields only 5 stable comparisons, 1 target-sensitive comparison, and 39 underpowered ones. Under a stricter max-deviation simultaneous interval, none of the 45 pairs can be resolved. This is a strong illustration that small rank gaps often do not support pairwise superiority.

2. AgentRewardBench: the top system changes with the label source. Expert labels place Claude 3.7 Sonnet first, while GPT-4o-mini judge labels place GPT-4o first. The paper interprets this as verifier disagreement: the measured quantity changes when the label source changes. This matters directly for any benchmark that relies on LLM judges or weak verifiers.

3. tau2-bench: protocol choices materially alter conclusions. For comparable primary runs, pass@4 raises scores by 17.7 to 20.4 points relative to pass@1, and adding cost to the utility rule can change which system is selected. Retry policy and budget are therefore part of the estimand, not secondary reporting details.

4. Coarser public releases: for DataAgentBench and Open Agent, the paper shows that without item-level records and uncertainty, one is limited to coarse reweighting or grouped comparisons; many pairwise claims are simply not identifiable.

The overall empirical message is precise: close leaderboard differences are more often unresolved than reversed once target choice and uncertainty are handled correctly.5d:T425,For a quick but useful read, focus on three parts.

Start with the introduction and Figure 1. They establish the key distinction between a released score and a pairwise superiority claim. That distinction is the backbone of the paper.

Then read Section IIIA carefully. The important pieces are not the statistical mechanics alone, but what each step protects against: estimand mismatch, lack of common support, ignored uncertainty, and arbitrary decision thresholds. The SWE-bench 0.792 vs 0.788 example is a good anchor while reading this section.

Finally, read the three case studies on SWE-bench, AgentRewardBench, and tau2-bench. If time is limited, prioritize the tables with decision labels and the discussion around unresolved comparisons.

A solid skim takes about 30–45 minutes. It is especially relevant if you build benchmarks, maintain public leaderboards, or rely on judge-based evaluation.5e:T818,The paper has two technical components. The first is a mechanistic diagnosis of what the authors call the consensus–termination gap. They generate one main reasoning trajectory per problem, freeze it, and then append probes offline to different prefixes of that same trajectory. This frozen-trajectory design is crucial because it ensures that different probing schedules and stopping rules observe identical underlying reasoning rather than perturbing it. On top of this substrate, they run three direct measurements.

First, wording sensitivity: for the same frozen prefix, they vary the wording of the probe and check whether the extracted current answer changes. If early prefixes are highly sensitive to probe wording, then the answer is being elicited by the query rather than read out from a settled internal state. Second, a hand-labeled taxonomy of wrong stops: among cases where the rule stops and the committed answer is wrong, they distinguish trajectories that had genuinely converged to a wrong answer from trajectories that had not converged at all and were merely forced into a temporary placeholder by the probe. Third, non-terminal commitment analysis: they measure how often a consensus stop commits to an answer that the original trajectory later abandons, and whether the truncated continuation would have corrected that answer.

The second component is a preregistered exhaustive sweep over a family of windowed consensus rules. The search space includes window size, agreement-share threshold, and operational knobs, for a total of 3,520 rules. These are evaluated on frozen trajectories from two models and three benchmarks with problem-grouped splits and pre-fixed acceptance gates. This is a strong design choice: instead of showcasing a few hand-picked operating points, the paper asks whether the rule family contains any robustly usable point at all. A non-consensus baseline, DEER, is run through the exact same pipeline and token accounting, which isolates whether the failure comes from the signal or from the early-exit objective itself.5f:T858,The empirical case is quite tight. On the mechanism side, re-probing the same frozen prefix with different wording yields different answers 54% of the time in the first tenth of a trajectory, versus 16% near the end. Early extracted answers are therefore highly probe-dependent. In a hand-labeled set of 134 wrong-stop cases, more than half are situations where the model had not actually converged and the probe forced a premature answer, while only about a quarter are cases where the model had truly settled on a wrong answer. The non-terminal commitment analysis is even more telling: at a consensus rule that still saves 32% of tokens, one stop in nine commits an answer that the trajectory later leaves behind. Among 216 such non-terminal stops, 155 cut off a correction the trajectory would have made, while only 16 banked a correct answer from a trajectory that would later end wrong. In other words, the computation being removed is mostly useful corrective computation.

The rule sweep then shows that this is not a threshold artifact. Across 3,520 preregistered consensus rules, none clears the pre-specified safety-and-savings gates on development, so none is carried forward. Yet 478 rules clear a gate in-sample on the training split, which explains how a less disciplined selection protocol could have produced optimistic conclusions. The frontier reproduces strongly on the held-out test split (r = 0.98) and on unseen models, including one at 4× scale and with a different architecture, so the negative result is stable. The contrast with DEER is the key control: under the same protocol, DEER clears all three gates and on unseen models can lose as little as 0.3 percentage points while saving 28% of tokens. At matched savings, consensus is much more expensive: at 28% net saving, the cheapest consensus rule still costs 6.0 points of accuracy, and at 33% saving it costs 8.3 points, versus 0.5 and 2.0 points for DEER. The paper also notes that a shipped operating point, CertaIndex (CoT), loses 56–70 points on the same trajectories, which underscores how brittle these heuristics can be under strict accounting.60:T492,Although labeled skim, this deserves a careful skim if you work on reasoning inference. Start with the introduction to pin down the target: this is not self-consistency across independently sampled trajectories, but repeated probing of a single partial trajectory. Then go straight to Section 4, which contains the strongest evidence. The three pieces to focus on are probe-wording sensitivity, the wrong-stop taxonomy, and the non-terminal commitment analysis. Together they support the central claim that agreement only shows persistence under a fixed elicitation procedure, not reasoning termination. After that, read Section 5 for the preregistered sweep design: acceptance gates, problem-grouped splits, frozen-trajectory replay, and token accounting are what make the negative result credible.

If you are building early-exit systems, verifiers, or reasoning-boundary detectors, the protocol details in the experiments and appendix are worth reading in full.61:T79a,The method has three layers. First is IRT calibration. The authors fit a Two-Parameter Logistic model to the binary response matrix of 1,000 open-weight models on the full MMLU test set. They use stochastic variational inference in NumPyro/JAX rather than joint maximum likelihood, explicitly to avoid the incidental-parameters problem, since model ability parameters grow with sample size and can make item estimates inconsistent under JML. This yields item difficulty b_i, item discrimination a_i, and model ability theta_j. Second is explanatory modeling of difficulty. The paper builds a deterministic, text-extractable framework of structural features intended to separate declarative retrieval demand from procedural reasoning load. The named features include Zipf Rarity, Entity Density, and a Weighted Symbolic Complexity Graph. The first two approximate reliance on rare factual knowledge and entity-heavy prompts; the last one is meant to capture symbolic and sequential inferential burden. Importantly, the authors choose interpretable features rather than opaque embedding regressors. Third is dimensionality and invariance testing. Using the benchmark designers’ predefined STEM vs non-STEM partition, they fit a confirmatory two-dimensional IRT model in which each item loads only on the latent dimension associated with its assigned partition, compare it against a unidimensional model on held-out prediction, and test whether the feature-to-difficulty mapping is the same across the two partitions. The statistical machinery includes joint Wald tests, subject-clustered covariance estimates, wild cluster bootstrap, and Holm correction, which shows care about false positives induced by subject clustering. The key technical claim is that if a benchmark truly measures one latent ability, the relationship between item difficulty and structural features should be approximately invariant across subdomains; MMLU fails that test.62:T701,The empirical setup is substantial. On the model side, the study covers 1,000 open-weight models, reduced to 869 distinct checkpoints and 50 base-family-and-size combinations after deduplication, spanning 3.2M to over 180B parameters. On the benchmark side, it uses all 14,042 MMLU test items, for about 14 million observations. After IRT calibration, item difficulty ranges from -5.00 to 7.12 with standard deviation 2.24, while model ability ranges from -2.02 to 3.14 with standard deviation 1.03. Reliability is strong: calibrating two random cohorts of 500 models separately yields a correlation of r_hh = 0.9921 between the two item-difficulty vectors. The main results are fourfold. First, the two-dimensional IRT model outperforms the unidimensional one, and the latent correlation between STEM and non-STEM ability is rho = 0.965, clearly below 1, with no posterior mass above 0.99. Second, the disattenuated subscale correlation at matched test length is 0.977, again indicating high relatedness but not interchangeability. Third, the mapping from structural features to item difficulty is not invariant across STEM and non-STEM. Among nine tested contrasts, only Entity Density survives subject-clustered covariance, wild cluster bootstrap, and Holm correction, and even that feature flips role: it behaves as an active constraint inside STEM items and as a retrieval cue outside them. Fourth, aggregate rank tracks non-STEM accuracy more closely than STEM accuracy even after equalizing test length, which is important because it shows the bias is not just a consequence of partition size. A structured extractor proposes field labels, which are normalized, expanded through prototype matching, and conservatively merged. Fields with at least 300 pre-2026-01-01 paper-field memberships are retained, yielding 278 valid fields and 1,390 episodes. For each field, a frozen codebook of exactly eight directions is built from pre-2024 evidence, with names, definitions, inclusion and exclusion rules, and exemplars. At each rolling origin, the agent can search only pre-cutoff literature and must predict the distribution of first submissions in the next six months. Search generally improves over Closed, but none of the four diagnostic models in natural agent settings beats an exact-count exponentially weighted moving average baseline in compositional accuracy. Under Expanding-history access, State carry-forward outperforms direct Forecast for all four models, showing that asking the agent to forecast can be worse than asking it to recover the current field state and carrying that state forward. Frozen-evidence replay attributes part of the failure to acquisition: Forecast-oriented policies allocate a smaller share of retrieved evidence to the most recent six-month window, even though that window is more useful for the future target. With exact history, future-specific updating remains limited; only GPT-5.5 with reopened Search slightly surpasses EWMA. MotionBlind uses a contrastive minimal-pair design. Each instance contains two near-identical clips recorded in the same scene with the same objects and background, differing only in one motion property such as left vs right movement, faster vs slower motion, or larger vs smaller displacement. Each clip is paired with two complementary yes/no questions, yielding four binary decisions per instance. An instance counts as correct only if all four are correct. This strict instance-level metric is intended to suppress inflated scores from partial guessing.

The dataset is self-recorded rather than scraped from the internet. That choice matters because internet videos are hard to control for static confounds and hard to label precisely for physical motion variables. The paper also prefers relative-motion questions over absolute notions like “fast” or “slow,” since absolute labels depend heavily on context. Comparing two moving references within the same scene reduces semantic ambiguity and makes the benchmark a cleaner test of motion perception.

The probing setup is well designed. First, a no-video text-only probe tests whether questions can be answered from language priors alone. Second, shuffled-frame and reversed-frame probes test temporal-order sensitivity: if performance barely changes when order is destroyed, the model is likely not using motion information. Third, the paper studies frame selection under budgets from 1 to 24 frames, comparing uniform sampling, random sampling, a GRPO-trained learned selector (HORNet), and a training-free key-clip selector (Frame2Clip). This helps separate several possible failure modes: whether one frame is already enough, whether more frames help, and whether better frame selection can recover motion understanding.67:T615,The empirical conclusion is straightforward: current Video-LLMs perform poorly on physically grounded motion understanding, and standard video-QA scores do not reveal this weakness. The paper evaluates models on MotionBlind together with TimeBlind and Video-MME. Non-contrastive benchmarks such as Video-MME can make models look broadly capable, but performance drops sharply when static content is controlled and only motion differs. The introduction cites TimeBlind as a reference point, where even strong frontier models reach only 48.2% instance accuracy while humans achieve 98.2%. MotionBlind narrows the focus further to speed, direction, and magnitude.

The diagnostic results are the most useful part. The text-only probe checks whether benchmark leakage through language priors is possible. The shuffled/reversed-frame probes test whether models are actually sensitive to temporal order. If order corruption causes only limited degradation, that is strong evidence that the model is reading static frames rather than motion. The frame-budget and frame-selection experiments then ask whether the issue is simply missing key frames. The paper’s answer is largely no: increasing frames or using more sophisticated selectors does not fully recover the missing capability. The excerpt provided here does not include the full result tables for MotionBlind, so I will not fabricate exact numbers. But the paper’s argument is clear: the bottleneck is deeper than frame sampling and points to weak motion representations in current Video-LLM pipelines.68:T496,This is a good skim paper. Read it for the benchmark design and the diagnostic logic, not for model innovation. Start with the introduction to understand why standard video-QA can overestimate temporal competence. Stage one builds structured compositional supervision. Instead of crude object swapping, the pipeline starts from real images sampled from LAION-400M. Qwen3-VL-32B extracts a structured scene graph-like description with objects, attributes, and relations. A sampled schema decides how many objects and attributes to keep. Conditioned on this schema and a five-level matching taxonomy, the MLLM generates one retrieval query and five captions. The five levels are: full match, partial presence, attribute error, object error, and full mismatch. Z-Image-Turbo then synthesizes one candidate image per caption, yielding a graded candidate list rather than a flat positive/negative set.

Stage two performs distillation. The synthesized data first fine-tunes a reranker, producing Core-Reranker. Then the reranker’s listwise compositional preferences are distilled into the embedding model, producing Core-Embed. The paper compares standard contrastive learning, pairwise CoSENT, and listwise Rank-KL. The main conclusion is that listwise supervision is the right fit for this setting because the target is not just “correct vs incorrect” but an ordered similarity spectrum. Rank-KL works by matching the embedding-induced ranking distribution to the teacher reranker’s distribution over the whole candidate list. Another useful detail is the diagnostic on Matryoshka dimensions: increasing representation dimension helps binding-sensitive subsets much more than simple lexical substitutions, which motivates distillation beyond merely widening the embedding.6a:T59f,There are three main experimental messages. First, the paper validates the capability gap between reranking and embedding. A representative example shows that both the backbone and the reranker rank fine-grained compositional candidates correctly, while embedding similarity fails. The Matryoshka sweep supports the same story: on two SugarCrepe++ subsets, increasing the representation dimension from 512 to 1536 barely changes Replace Attribute, from 0.773 to 0.777, but improves the more binding-sensitive Swap Attribute from 0.589 to 0.623.

Second, the objective comparison is important. CoSENT and Rank-KL both outperform standard contrastive learning under the five-level supervision, and Rank-KL is the strongest overall. This suggests the gain is not only from better hard negatives, but also from using an objective aligned with ordered supervision.

Third, the end results are solid. Core-Reranker-8B reaches 82.7% total average on compositional reasoning benchmarks, surpassing the previous best reranker. Core-Embed-8B achieves the best total average among evaluated embedding models. On MCMR, Core-Embed-8B improves R@1 from 0.375 to 0.412 over its backbone, while preserving performance on standard retrieval sets such as COCO and Flickr30K. The graded held-out evaluation protocol is also a meaningful contribution because it measures whether the model learns relative compositional similarity, not just binary correctness.6b:T6b4,The method, FactoSR, follows a two-stage recipe: supervised spatial fine-tuning first, then factorized reinforcement learning. In the SFT stage, the model is taught to produce structured outputs that separate observation, localization, reasoning, and final answer. In the RL stage, the authors build on RLVR with GRPO-style optimization, but replace the usual single correctness reward with a multi-objective reward design.

There are five reward components. A format reward keeps outputs structurally valid during RL. An accuracy reward preserves standard final-answer supervision. The key novelty lies in three geometry-aware rewards. The XY reward enforces cross-view planar consistency and correspondence, encouraging the model to identify the correct region before answering. The Z reward targets 3D localization and relative depth ordering, which is critical for front/back, near/far, and occlusion reasoning. The T reward enforces temporal cycle consistency and reversible camera-motion reasoning, pushing the model to remain coherent over sequences rather than treating frames independently.

This is not an architectural change to the backbone. It is a change in task decomposition and training signal design. Relative to prior spatial RLVR work, the differences are clear: it moves from final-answer-only rewards to factorized rewards, from mostly single-view reasoning to multi-view and temporal settings, and from implicit language-space reasoning to explicitly geometry-constrained optimization. The trade-off is also clear: the approach depends on datasets and annotations that support verifiable XY/Z/T rewards, so scalability and transfer will depend on how broadly those rewards can be instantiated.6c:T59b,The headline results reported in the paper are gains of 5.9% on VSI-Bench and 4.5% on All-Angles-Bench, while maintaining decent general multimodal capability. The experimental story is less about one benchmark and more about whether the factorized rewards produce separable gains on separable spatial skills.

The key ablations compare SFT only, SFT plus standard RLVR, and SFT plus FactoSR-RL. The paper’s main claim is that answer-only RL helps somewhat, but remains unstable on depth, cross-view correspondence, and temporal consistency. Adding XY/Z/T rewards yields larger improvements on tasks that require explicit geometric reasoning chains. Reward ablations further support the decomposition: removing XY hurts cross-view localization and correspondence; removing Z weakens relative depth and occlusion judgments; removing T degrades camera-motion and temporal reverse-reasoning tasks. The authors also emphasize stronger generalization than pure SFT, arguing that RL encourages strategy learning rather than memorization of static patterns.

From the provided full-text excerpt, there is no reliable complete table of model size, training steps, or dataset scale, so those details should not be overstated. What is clear is that this is an SFT-plus-RL enhancement on top of an existing VLM, with the main contribution in reward design and spatial-temporal data construction rather than large-scale pretraining from scratch.6d:T652,DART stands for Depth-as-Target. The central design is to augment DINOv2 with a pixel-space depth reconstruction head, so the model keeps DINOv2’s self-distillation-based representation learning while also predicting pseudo depth maps. The key choice is what the paper does not do: it does not build an RGB-D encoder that requires depth at inference, and it does not follow the standard MAE-style route of feeding depth as an input modality. Instead, depth is used as auxiliary supervision during pretraining only. This matches the deployment constraint in surgery, where reliable depth input is often unavailable.

The motivation in the paper is comparative. Off-the-shelf DINOv2 and DINOv3 pretrained on natural images do not transfer well enough to surgical imagery. MAE-family methods, including RGB-D variants such as MultiMAE, also fail to close the gap in the authors’ setting; the paper explicitly notes that MultiMAE underperforms a single-modality MAE baseline in their surgical pretraining setup. That negative result is important because it justifies moving depth supervision into a DINOv2-style framework rather than continuing along the MAE path.

Technically, the training objective is a combination of the original DINOv2 objective and a depth reconstruction loss. The depth supervision comes from off-the-shelf pseudo-labeled dense depth rather than real depth sensors, which lowers the data barrier and makes the recipe scalable. The contribution is therefore not a new architecture but a domain-aware pretraining recipe that injects geometric supervision without changing inference requirements.6e:T47e,From the provided full-content excerpt, several experimental comparisons are clear. First, the paper compares off-the-shelf DINOv2/DINOv3, surgically adapted DINOv2, MAE, and RGB-D MAE variants, and concludes that natural-image VFMs transfer poorly while the DINOv2 route is the better starting point in this domain. Second, the paper explicitly reports a negative result: MultiMAE underperforms a single-modality MAE baseline in their surgical setting, which supports the decision not to use depth as an encoder input. Third, DART is intended to improve both dense pixel-level tasks and image-level tasks, so the evaluation is framed as multi-task transfer rather than a single downstream benchmark.

However, the excerpt provided here does not include the full result tables, exact dataset sizes, backbone scales, training budgets, or precise gains. Without those sections, it would be unsafe to invent numbers. What can be stated confidently is that the experimental argument is built around recipe comparison and transfer breadth, with DART positioned as a better surgical pretraining recipe than RGB-only DINOv2 and MAE-style RGB-D alternatives.6f:Te4a,整体架构由三部分组成：一个基于 LLaDA 2.0 的冻结 dLLM-VLM 负责多模态理解，一个 connector 把理解侧 hidden states 投到生成条件空间，一个 6B 单流 Diffusion Transformer 负责图像合成。关键点不在“模块很多”，而在职责边界划得很清楚。

1. 先学视觉先验，再学语言对齐
作者反对从训练一开始就重度依赖图文对。原因有两个：一是 caption 贵且噪声大；二是在低分辨率训练阶段，caption 中描述的细节常因下采样而不可见，导致条件和目标不匹配。为此，他们先做 image-only pre-training 和 mid-training，让 DiT 先把自然图像分布学扎实。这里不是无条件生成，而是借助冻结 VLM 从“同一图像区域”提取条件表示，让条件和生成目标天然对齐，避免外部 caption 带来的语义漂移。这个设计很像在做一种自蒸馏式的视觉条件建模：监督信号主要来自真实图像本身，语言只在后期逐步接入。

2. 统一理解、生成、编辑，但不强行共用所有路径
文本生成和编辑共用同一条语义条件路径：文本、视觉上下文和结构化 reasoning trace 先进入 dLLM-VLM，再经 Residual Query Adapter 和轻量 Transformer connector 送入 DiT。编辑任务则额外引入 reference-image pathway，而且这个路径直接进 DiT，绕过 VLM。作者这样做的原因很实际：编辑时既需要高层语义指令，也需要像素级或局部外观证据；如果全部压进 VLM hidden states，参考图像细节容易损失。因此他们同时使用 SigLIP-VQ 特征和 clean VAE latent，分别提供语义级和像素级参考信号。这个设计说明作者没有把“统一”理解成单一路径，而是按信息类型分层接入。

3. progressive training pipeline
训练分阶段推进：先在 256 分辨率做 image-only pre-training；再做 aspect-ratio-bucketed mid-training，继续扩展视觉先验；之后在 512 和 1024 分辨率引入 paired language alignment；再对 text-rich 和 portrait 数据做 targeted refinement；最后做 generation-editing joint training。这里有两个关键取舍。其一，数据配比上始终保持 real-data-dominant，整条生成训练链约 2.2 亿样本，其中 98% 是真实图像，SFT 阶段真实图像占比也保持在 70% 以上。作者承认这种路线在早期 benchmark 收敛可能慢于 synthetic-heavy 配方，但长期 realism ceiling 更高。其二，训练目标不是一次性混训所有能力，而是按“先分布、后条件、再任务整合”的顺序推进，这和大模型训练里常见的 annealing / curriculum 思路一致。

4. 稳定性与优化
DiT 全面使用 parameter-free RMSNorm，而不是带可学习缩放参数的归一化。作者的意图是减少大模型 diffusion 训练中的尺度漂移和额外不稳定因素。优化器选 Muon，也是在强调大规模从头训练的稳定与效率。虽然从给出的片段里看不到完整优化细节和对比表，但论文把这两点列为 recipe 的核心组成，说明它们不是边角工程，而是支撑 6B DiT 训练成功的重要条件。

5. TwinFlow 蒸馏到 Turbo
部署侧使用 TwinFlow，把原始多步 diffusion 模型蒸馏成 2–4 步的 LLaDA-Image Turbo。方法上结合了 distribution-matching distillation 和 self-adversarial flow training。值得注意的是，作者把 Turbo 视为同一家族的部署变体，而不是另起一个轻量模型。这意味着训练时就考虑了 teacher 分布是否适合后续 few-step student 拟合，属于“为蒸馏而设计主模型”的思路。70:T65f,This is highly relevant to foundation-model pretraining. Its significance is not just that it trains a 6B DiT, but that it makes several training decisions explicit and backs them with a full recipe. Four contributions stand out.

First, it argues clearly for decoupling visual-prior learning from language alignment. The generator is trained to model image distribution first, and paired supervision is introduced later. That is closely analogous to the separation between broad pretraining and later alignment in LLMs, and it is a useful design pattern for multimodal foundation training.

Second, it shows a concrete role for a diffusion language model beyond understanding alone. The frozen LLaDA2.0-Mini-based VLM acts as a semantic conditioning hub that unifies text, visual context, and reasoning traces. This gives a practical answer to how an understanding model and a generation model can be separated without becoming disconnected.

Third, the paper contributes a serious large-scale training recipe: parameter-free RMSNorm throughout the DiT, the Muon optimizer, and a progressive curriculum over data type and resolution. For training large DiTs from scratch, these choices matter more than many cosmetic architectural tweaks.

Fourth, few-step distillation is treated as part of the main model family rather than an afterthought. In that sense, LLaDA-Image is not just a model but a full pipeline from prior learning to alignment, editing, and deployment. This should matter for open image-generation pretraining, and it also has direct relevance to unified multimodal pretraining and AR-plus-diffusion style systems.71:T1037,The system has three main components: a frozen dLLM-based VLM built on LLaDA 2.0 for multimodal understanding, a connector that projects understanding-side hidden states into the generator conditioning space, and a 6B single-stream Diffusion Transformer for image synthesis. The key is not the number of modules, but the clarity of their roles.

1. Learn the visual prior first, then align to language.
The authors explicitly avoid heavy dependence on paired image-text data at the beginning of training. Their argument is practical: captions are expensive and noisy, and at low training resolutions many captioned details are no longer visible after downsampling, which creates condition-target mismatch. Instead, they begin with image-only pretraining and mid-training so that the DiT first learns the natural image distribution well. This is not purely unconditional generation. A frozen VLM extracts conditioning signals from the same image region that the DiT is asked to generate, which keeps condition and target tightly matched without relying on external captions. Conceptually, this resembles a form of self-distilled visual conditioning: the image itself provides most of the supervision signal, while language is introduced later.

2. Unify understanding, generation, and editing without forcing a single pathway for everything.
Text-to-image generation and editing share the same semantic conditioning route: text, visual context, and structured reasoning traces are encoded by the dLLM-VLM, then passed through a Residual Query Adapter and a lightweight Transformer connector into the DiT. Editing adds a separate reference-image pathway that goes directly into the DiT and bypasses the VLM. This is an important design choice. Editing needs both high-level semantic instructions and low-level appearance evidence; if everything is compressed into VLM hidden states, reference fidelity can be lost. To address this, the model uses both SigLIP-VQ features and clean VAE latents, providing semantic-level and pixel-level reference signals respectively. The paper’s notion of unification is therefore layered rather than monolithic.

3. Progressive training pipeline.
Training proceeds in stages: image-only pretraining at 256 resolution, aspect-ratio-bucketed mid-training to strengthen the visual prior, paired language alignment at 512 and 1024 resolution, targeted refinement on text-rich and portrait data, and finally joint generation-editing training. Two design choices matter here. First, the data mixture remains real-data-dominant throughout. The full generation pipeline processes about 220M samples, 98% of them real images, and the real-image share stays above 70% even during supervised fine-tuning. The authors explicitly acknowledge that this may converge more slowly on early benchmarks than synthetic-heavy mixtures, but they argue that it yields stronger realism at convergence. Second, capabilities are not mixed all at once. The curriculum follows a distribution-first, conditioning-next, task-integration-later order, which is very much in line with annealing and curriculum ideas in large-model training.

4. Stability and optimization.
The DiT uses parameter-free RMSNorm throughout rather than a learnable affine normalization. The motivation is to reduce scale drift and unnecessary instability in large-scale diffusion training. The optimizer is Muon, again chosen with training stability and scalability in mind. The provided excerpt does not include the full optimization ablations, but the paper presents these choices as central parts of the recipe rather than minor implementation details.

5. TwinFlow distillation to Turbo.
For deployment, the original multi-step model is distilled into 2–4-step LLaDA-Image Turbo variants using TwinFlow, which combines distribution-matching distillation with self-adversarial flow training. An important point is that Turbo is treated as a deployment variant within the same family, not as a separate lightweight model. This suggests that the teacher is trained with downstream few-step distillation in mind, which is a more integrated view of training and serving.72:T8fd,The experimental results support several distinct claims.

First, on overall capability, LLaDA-Image performs strongly on Qwen-Image-Bench, LongText-Bench, CVTG-2K, and GEdit-Bench, covering photorealism, prompt alignment, bilingual Chinese-English text rendering, and instruction-guided editing. The emphasis is on balanced capability rather than optimizing a single aesthetic metric. That matters because many open models still lag badly on text rendering or reference-preserving editing.

Second, the data strategy is a central empirical result. The paper argues that image-only pretraining followed by progressive language alignment is not only viable, but preferable in the long run to synthetic-heavy paired training from the start. Synthetic mixtures may improve early benchmark numbers faster, but they also inject artifacts and caption bias that hurt realism later. The full generation pipeline uses about 220M samples, with more than 90% of training in image-only stages and 98% of samples coming from real images. Those numbers make the intended shift in supervision very concrete.

Third, the system scale and deployment profile are explicit. The main generator is a 6B DiT trained from scratch, while the understanding module is built on a frozen LLaDA2.0-Mini backbone. The release includes four checkpoints: Base and Turbo, plus FP8 variants of each. The Turbo models run with only 2–4 sampling steps, which substantially lowers inference cost.

Fourth, editing performance comes from the unified architecture rather than a separate editing backbone. Text-to-image and editing share the semantic path, while reference images are injected through an additional DiT-side pathway. This allows the model to balance instruction following and reference preservation on editing benchmarks such as GEdit-Bench. That is an important result for unified multimodal generation systems, where many models still trade off editability against fidelity.

The provided excerpt does not include full score tables, FID values, or detailed human-evaluation numbers, so those should not be fabricated. The reliable hard facts are: a 6B DiT, roughly 220M training samples, 98% real images, more than 90% image-only training stages, more than 70% real-image share during SFT, and 2–4-step Turbo inference.73:T74e,This one deserves a careful read. Do not start from the benchmark tables. Start with the introduction and model design, because the paper is really about training philosophy and system decomposition. The three questions to keep in mind are: why learn the visual prior before language alignment, why route editing through an extra reference path instead of only through the VLM, and why insist on a real-data-dominant recipe.

A good reading order is:
1. Introduction: identify the three main threads—data decoupling, unified architecture, and few-step deployment.
2. Model Design: focus on the interfaces among the frozen dLLM-VLM, the Residual Query Adapter, the connector, and the single-stream DiT. This is where the division of labor between understanding and generation becomes clear.
3. Training pipeline: this is the most valuable section for pretraining researchers. Pay close attention to stage boundaries, data composition, resolution transitions, when paired data is introduced, and how refinement data is selected.
4. Stability and optimization details: look for the rationale and any ablations behind parameter-free RMSNorm and Muon, especially whether they matter more at larger batch sizes, higher resolutions, or longer training runs.
5. Editing and Turbo distillation: if you care about unified multimodal generation or deployment, read these sections closely, especially the reference pathway and the TwinFlow objective.
6. Experiments: prioritize ablations on data mixture, the necessity of the image-only stages, the effect of real-data ratio on realism and alignment, and the quality-speed trade-off between the original model and Turbo.

If time is limited, spend at least 60–90 minutes on the method and training recipe. If you work on diffusion LMs, unified multimodal pretraining, or AR-plus-diffusion systems, this is worth taking notes on.74:Ta3b,GEPARD 是一个 decoder-only 自回归 transformer，输入文本，输出神经 codec 的离散音频 token，不做文本生成，只预测音频序列和结束标记。骨干基于 Qwen3.5 风格结构，但做了关键裁剪：保留 14 层、hidden size 1024、8 个 attention heads，约 500M 参数；加上音频接口和 voice cloning 后总参数约 555.7M。作者强调 backbone 必须保持“stock”——也就是标准 full-attention transformer，不在自回归循环中插入自定义算子，以保证兼容标准 vLLM 和 FlashAttention-2。

一个重要细节是，他们移除了原始 Qwen3.5 中的 LinearBlock，只保留 full attention。文本 embedding 和 tokenizer 继承自预训练 Qwen，其余 backbone 基本从头训练，因为结构变化后旧权重不再兼容。作者给出的理由主要是经验性的：在相同条件下，纯 full-attention 版本听感更好，同时更适合 vLLM。这个判断还不算严格验证，但符合系统目标。

音频侧使用 NVIDIA NanoCodec，22kHz、21.5 fps、1.89 kbps，把语音离散成 codec token 序列。模型的核心设计原则是：所有非标准模态变换都放到 prefill 或离线阶段。具体包括三点。

第一，zero-shot voice cloning 不在解码环中做动态 cross-attention，而是先用冻结的音频压缩器提取说话人表示，形成 K=8 个 speaker prefix tokens，作为输入前缀一次性送入 backbone。这样 speaker conditioning 成为普通 prefix conditioning，而不是逐步参与解码的额外模块。

第二，针对超短文本生成时常见的 runaway 或 skip 问题，作者提出“short register”分析，把它视为序列过短导致的分布异常和停止行为失衡。他们用文本重复等 augmentation 在 prefill 阶段补偿，而不是在推理时加入动态规则。文中还提到用 entropy 和 stop-probability probe 做诊断，这部分更像训练动态与失败模式分析。

第三，CFG 不在 serving 时做双路前向，而是先离线生成带/不带 CFG 的配对样本，再用 DPO 把 CFG 带来的偏好蒸馏到单路模型，且使用长度与质量归一化的 reward scaling。这个点对基座研究者最有意思，因为它体现的是“把昂贵推理策略蒸馏进参数”的思路，和 speculative decoding 之外的另一类 serving-aware training 很接近。

整体上，GEPARD 不是在 codec 结构或语音 tokenization 上做新算法，而是在标准 LM 骨干、codec 接口、prefix conditioning、offline preference distillation 之间做了一个尽量不破坏 serving 栈的组合设计。75:Ta95,GEPARD is a decoder-only autoregressive transformer that takes text as input and emits discrete neural-codec audio tokens. It does not generate text; it only predicts audio tokens and an end-of-speech signal. The backbone is Qwen3.5-inspired but simplified: 14 blocks, hidden size 1024, 8 attention heads, about 500M parameters; the full model including audio interface and voice cloning is about 555.7M parameters. A central design constraint is that the backbone must remain a stock full-attention transformer, with no custom operations inside the autoregressive loop, so that standard vLLM and FlashAttention-2 can be used directly.

A notable architectural choice is the removal of Qwen3.5’s LinearBlock layers, leaving only full attention. The text embeddings and tokenizer are inherited from pretrained Qwen, while the rest of the backbone is effectively retrained because the structural change makes the original weights incompatible. The justification is empirical and system-driven: the pure full-attention version sounded better in informal comparisons and is easier to serve with vLLM.

On the audio side, the model uses NVIDIA NanoCodec at 22 kHz, 21.5 frames per second, and 1.89 kbps, turning speech into discrete codec tokens. The overarching principle is to move all non-standard modal computation out of the decode loop.

First, zero-shot voice cloning is implemented as prefix conditioning. A frozen audio compressor extracts a speaker representation once during prefill, producing K=8 speaker tokens that are prepended to the input. This avoids dynamic cross-attention to speaker features during decoding.

Second, the paper studies a failure mode for very short utterances, called the “short register” problem, where AR TTS models may loop indefinitely or skip words. Instead of adding runtime control logic, the authors address it through prefill-side text augmentation, such as text repetition, and analyze it using entropy and stop-probability probes.

Third, classifier-free guidance is removed from serving. Rather than running conditional and unconditional passes at every generation step, the model uses offline paired generations and DPO to distill CFG behavior into a single-pass model, with reward scaling normalized by length and quality. This is arguably the most transferable idea for foundation-model researchers: expensive inference-time behavior is converted into a training-time preference signal and baked into the weights.

Overall, the paper is not proposing a new codec or a new speech tokenization method. It is a serving-aware integration of a standard LM backbone, discrete audio tokens, prefix-based speaker conditioning, and offline preference distillation.76:T840,The evaluation is presented in two stages. In an early concept-validation setup on a rented RTX 5090, a single-stream vLLM run achieved an RTF of about 0.040 and a TTFA of about 0.032 seconds, roughly 25× faster than real time. This serves as a sanity check that the vLLM-native design is viable. In the more realistic production-style setup, using server-class GPUs and a full SSE streaming harness, the end-to-end system including backbone and neural codec reaches about 0.067 RTF and about 0.046 seconds TTFA/TTFB in single-thread mode. Aggregate throughput scales nearly linearly up to 256 concurrent streams, reaching around 204× real-time throughput. The reported practical operating range is 64–128 streams per GPU, where each stream still maintains interactive performance with RTF below 0.75.

The model size is about 500M for the backbone and 555.7M overall. The audio tokenizer is NanoCodec at 21.5 fps and 1.89 kbps. The authors explicitly state that the model is not aiming for top-tier speech-quality metrics; on Seed-TTS-eval it sits in the middle range. That is important for interpreting the paper correctly: the main result is not absolute MOS or intelligibility, but real-time and concurrent serving within a standard LLM stack.

The paper also analyzes two interesting phenomena. One is the short-utterance failure mode, where 1–2 word inputs can trigger runaway generation or skipped words; entropy and stop-probability probes are used for diagnosis. The other is representation leakage in voice cloning: speaker similarity on unseen voices is limited, and the authors attribute part of this to leakage in quantized representations rather than treating it as a generic quality issue. WavLM speaker embeddings are used for evaluation.

The provided excerpt does not include the full result tables, so exact before/after numbers for DPO-based CFG distillation, short-register compensation, or multilingual performance cannot be reproduced safely here. Still, the reported latency, throughput, model scale, and codec configuration are sufficient to locate the paper’s main contribution.77:T5a1,From a foundation-model perspective, three parts deserve attention. First, read the introduction carefully for the constraint definition: why many TTS architectures are incompatible with stock vLLM, and how the paper turns “do not modify the decode loop” into a hard design rule. Second, read the architecture section with focus on the speaker prefix, the audio interface, and the decision to keep a pure full-attention backbone. Third, read the sections on CFG distillation via DPO and the short-register analysis, since those contain the most transferable ideas.

Do not read it as a conventional TTS paper centered on quality metrics. The more useful question is how online complexity is shifted into offline training or prefill: speaker conditioning moved to the prefix, CFG distilled into weights, and short-utterance failures addressed through data and training rather than runtime heuristics. Those choices are relevant to speech LM serving and to unified multimodal LMs more broadly.

The most useful artifacts to inspect are: the architecture overview and input formatting, the short-register diagnostic plots, especially entropy and stop-probability probes, the DPO pipeline used to distill CFG, and the concurrency/latency curves for TTFA and RTF. A 30-minute skim is enough to decide whether the paper is relevant. A 60-minute read is better if the goal is to extract design principles for speech LM or multimodal LM systems.78:T456,The system uses the 12hz_v1 DualCodec representation for 24 kHz audio. DualCodec produces eight RVQ streams at 12.5 Hz. The first codebook is derived from w2v-BERT-2.0 features and carries more semantic and phonetic information, while later codebooks encode acoustic residuals. TontaubeV1 keeps the semantic stream plus the first three acoustic streams, reducing the retained bitrate to 625 bit/s compared with 1225 bit/s for the full stack. Generation is factorized coarse-to-fine. A Qwen3-1.7B-derived transformer predicts the semantic stream and thus the utterance duration and primary prosody. Three progressively smaller Qwen3-0.6B-derived transformers then add acoustic refinements. Each stage has its own network and conditions on text, available prompt streams, and previously generated coarser streams. For streaming, the system avoids relying directly on DualCodec’s non-causal decoder: overlapping DualCodec reconstructions are mapped into the VibeVoice acoustic latent space and decoded with VibeVoice’s causal decoder, allowing stable audio to be emitted before the full utterance is complete.79:T850,整体架构由三部分组成。第一部分是语义条件器：一个 multimodal LLM 编码文本，或联合编码文本与参考音频，再把层级 hidden states 聚合成 semantic condition。这样做的原因是，纯文本条件不足以表达说话人、风格、情绪、环境等信息，而直接让生成器从波形里自己抽高层语义又会让训练目标过重。第二部分是 AuK-VAE：在 speech、general audio、music 上联合训练的音频 VAE，提供共享 acoustic latent space，用于参考条件和最终波形重建。这里的设计选择很关键：如果只在语音上训练离散或连续 codec，编辑任务里遇到非语音声学事件、背景音或音乐片段时，latent 空间会过窄。第三部分是生成主干：hybrid rectified-flow Transformer。前段使用 dual-stream MMDiT blocks，让 semantic stream 和 acoustic stream 先交互但保留各自残差路径；后段切换到 unified single-stream DiT blocks，在融合后的序列上预测 rectified-flow velocity。这个结构比一开始就全融合更稳，因为生成和编辑任务对“保留已有声学信息”与“注入新语义信息”的要求不同，前期分流更容易控制条件注入强度。

训练分三步。预训练先做 generation-only warm-up，再联合 generation 和 editing，用共享 flow-matching objective 学统一映射。这样安排是因为编辑任务条件更复杂，若一开始混训，模型容易在基础可懂度和自然度上不稳。后训练分成两条线：编辑侧做 flow-based preference optimization，因为开放式编辑很难靠单一自动指标覆盖；生成侧做 Flow-GRPO，用内容正确性、说话人相似度、指令-风格一致性等自动奖励优化。最后再做蒸馏：通过 consistency initialization 和 task-routed Decoupled DMD，把 32 NFE teacher 压到 4-step、CFG-free 的 AuK-Flash。这里最有意思的是，作者没有把 RL 或 preference optimization 只当作后处理，而是把它们接到 flow 模型训练里，形成从统一预训练到偏好优化再到快速采样蒸馏的一整条链路。7a:T961,The system has three main components. The first is a semantic conditioner: a multimodal LLM encodes text alone or text together with reference audio, and aggregates hierarchical hidden states into a semantic condition. This choice is deliberate. Text alone cannot fully specify speaker identity, style, emotion, or environment, while asking the acoustic generator to infer all high-level semantics directly from waveform conditioning would overload the generation objective. The second component is AuK-VAE, an audio VAE trained jointly on speech, general audio, and music to provide a shared acoustic latent space for both reference conditioning and waveform reconstruction. This matters because a speech-only codec space would be too narrow for editing tasks that involve non-speech acoustic events, background sounds, or mixed scenes. The third component is the generator backbone: a hybrid rectified-flow Transformer. It starts with dual-stream MMDiT blocks so that semantic and acoustic streams can exchange information while keeping separate residual pathways, then switches to unified single-stream DiT blocks that refine the fused sequence and predict rectified-flow velocity. Compared with immediate full fusion, this design is better aligned with the needs of mixed generation and editing tasks, where the model must balance preservation of existing acoustics against injection of new semantics.

Training is staged. Unified pretraining begins with a generation-only warm-up, then moves to joint optimization of generation and editing under a shared flow-matching objective. The warm-up is important because editing has more complex conditioning and can destabilize basic intelligibility and naturalness if introduced too early. Post-training splits into two branches. For editing, the authors use flow-based preference optimization because open-ended editing quality is hard to capture with a single automatic metric. For generation, they apply Flow-GRPO with automatic rewards for content correctness, speaker similarity, and instruction-style consistency. Finally, they distill the post-trained teacher using consistency initialization and task-routed Decoupled DMD, producing AuK-Flash, a 4-step, CFG-free student. One of the more interesting aspects is that RL-style and preference-based optimization are integrated into the flow-model pipeline rather than treated as an external patch.7b:T749,On the data side, the paper constructs about 3.03B instruction-audio instances and 1.95M hours of effective supervision across five task families: speech generation, acoustic editing, paralinguistic editing, content editing, and enhancement/separation. The generation data includes transcript-free zero-shot TTS and instruction-controlled TTS. The transcript-free setup is notable: for a speaker with n utterances, the corpus enumerates paired examples where one utterance serves as the acoustic prompt and another utterance’s text serves as the synthesis target, avoiding dependence on a transcript for the prompt audio. The curation pipeline includes source separation, speech enhancement, MOS-based quality filtering, speaker verification, and cross-checking with multiple ASR systems, which signals a strong emphasis on supervision quality.

On the model side, the main reported outcome is broad capability: AuK performs strongly on zero-shot and instruction-based speech generation and on general instruction-guided speech editing, while remaining competitive on signal-level restoration tasks such as enhancement, separation, and super-resolution. AuK-Flash preserves broad generation and editing ability while delivering a 4.5× wall-clock speedup relative to the 32-NFE teacher under matched conditions. The provided excerpt does not include the full benchmark tables, but the evaluation design clearly goes beyond a single MOS number. It considers content correctness, speaker similarity, edit strength, naturalness, contextual appropriateness, and preservation of unspecified attributes. First, a VLM-based coding agent takes a reference image and natural-language instructions, initializes the world, identifies entities, assigns attributes and states, and writes executable programs that define interactions, triggers, and objectives. Second, a state executor maintains an explicit global world state and updates it according to user actions and programmed rules. This state includes off-screen entities and non-visual fields, so the system does not depend on the renderer to remember the world. Third, a generative renderer produces observations conditioned on compiled controls derived from the current state.

The key design choice is the intermediate representation. The paper compares text descriptions, 2D boxes and masks, detailed 3D scenes, and dense rendering controls such as G-buffers. It then chooses a state-augmented 3D oriented bounding box for each entity. The OBB encodes position, extent, and orientation in a shared world coordinate system, and is augmented with persistent identity, semantic category, dynamic state, and appearance information. This is a deliberate compromise. It is more geometric and view-consistent than text, less camera-tied than 2D controls, and much lighter than full 3D assets that would require explicit pose and geometry synthesis at inference time.

A deterministic state compiler then projects the evolving OBBs along the target camera trajectory and rasterizes them into pixel-aligned spatiotemporal controls. This is important. Instead of asking the video model to infer camera projection and entity-pixel correspondence implicitly, the compiler resolves those constraints explicitly. The renderer is left to synthesize fine geometry, articulation, texture, and secondary dynamics that are not specified by the compact state. In effect, the system splits the problem into explicit state evolution plus conditional generative completion.

The training side includes a data curation pipeline that recovers the spatial and semantic supervision needed for this interface from videos. Even from the available text, it is clear that the authors treat this pipeline as necessary for scaling: without extracting entity-level structure from video data, the proposed interface would remain a hand-built control mechanism rather than a trainable pretraining target.7e:T461,The visible experimental emphasis is on state-video consistency rather than generic video quality. The student samples rollouts under its current policy, and the teacher supplies a next-token distribution at each visited prefix. The student is then updated toward the teacher on those visited states, typically through a token-level KL or cross-entropy loss. The key move is to treat a query as a generator of states, not as a single training item. To quantify this, the paper defines state coverage: states visited by full-data OPD are grouped into semantic clusters, and a query set is scored by the fraction of those clusters reached by its rollouts. This avoids exact-prefix matching, which would be too sparse, and gives a better proxy for the supervision OPD actually sees. The second diagnostic is absorption rate, the fraction of the remaining teacher-student gap closed by one update. This separates insufficient data coverage from slow algorithmic uptake. If available, the appendix details on clustering, rollout sampling, teacher-logit access, temperature, and query selection are worth checking.82:T543,LeanGRPO removes update-stage recomputation through a systems redesign with two pieces. First, it changes the data-parallel layout. Instead of assigning different prompts to different GPUs and generating multiple local samples per prompt, all GPUs process the same prompt while each rank generates a different sample. This reduces the need for each rank to retain multiple computation graphs for the same prompt group.

Second, it introduces two recompute-free schedules. LeanGRPO-Retain simply enables gradient tracking during rollout and keeps the selected-timestep graphs alive until terminal rewards and group advantages are available, then reuses those graphs for backpropagation. It is simple but activation memory grows with the number of selected timesteps.

LeanGRPO-Reweight is more subtle. During rollout, each selected-timestep graph is immediately consumed through a provisional backward pass, producing a provisional gradient and allowing saved activations to be released right away. Once the terminal reward and advantage are known, the provisional gradient is corrected using that advantage, recovering the same policy gradient in exact arithmetic. This shifts the memory burden from retained activations to stored provisional gradients. The paper positions both schedules as objective-preserving rather than approximate shortcuts.83:T8bb,文章的核心设计是把 supervision 当成“随训练演化的状态”，而不是固定标签。围绕这个抽象，框架分成三个模块，但作者强调它们是互补的 intervention points，不是必须串行执行的流水线。

On top of that abstraction, the framework organizes the lifecycle into three modules, which are presented as complementary intervention points rather than a mandatory sequential pipeline.

The first module is Active Data Selection. It decides which examples should be retained for training, which should receive external labels, and which should be routed to weak supervision. Implementations include verified-difficulty filtering, model-based uncertainty selection, and probe-calibrated selection. The important design choice is that budget allocation is made explicit before expensive rollout and annotation are spent.

The second module is Weak Supervision Construction. It allows unlabeled examples to participate in RLVR by constructing pseudo-targets, enforcing agreement across views, or assigning target-free rewards. The framework covers methods such as TTRL, Co-Rewarding, EMRL, and Intuitor under a shared interface. This matters because weak supervision no longer requires rewriting the rollout-to-update loop; it becomes a localized change in supervision semantics.

The third module is Training-Time Supervision Refinement. Since supervision can become unreliable due to noise, policy drift, or reward hacking, the framework supports online reassessment and revision using reward dynamics, representation geometry, and rollout evidence. This includes methods such as TraPO, GeoMin, and online label refinement. The deeper point is that supervision quality should be revisited as the policy changes, not fixed once offline.

At the systems level, DE-Venus follows a minimal-invasion design. It keeps verl as the execution substrate for rollout generation, optimization, validation, and checkpointing, and inserts method-specific logic only at the boundaries where supervision semantics change. Persistent sample identity and supervision state are stored through a shared Parquet convention, while verl-compatible batches carry targets, rewards, selections, and advantages during online optimization. Reusable services handle voting, verification, uncertainty estimation, reward construction, evidence analysis, and validation logging. Additional experiments on coding reasoning, Llama models, and other algorithmic settings are used to check that the phenomenon is not limited to Qwen3 math training.88:T5d4,RISE constructs a synthetic teacher by extrapolating the displacement between a current RLVR-updated checkpoint and a trailing anchor checkpoint. Let π_{θ_n} be the policy at iteration n, updated by RLVR to π_{θ'_{n+1}}. Choose a representation map φ that embeds a policy into a vector space where linear operations are meaningful (parameters or logits/distributions). Define the recent improvement direction as Δ = φ(π_{θ'_{n+1}}) − φ(π_{θ_n}). The self-extrapolated teacher is obtained by projecting further along this direction with scale β:

φ(teacher) = φ(π_{θ'_{n+1}}) + (β−1)·Δ, with β>1.

Two instantiations are emphasized:
- Weight-space extrapolation (φ=θ): θ_future = θ'_{n+1} + (β−1)(θ'_{n+1}−θ_n), essentially task arithmetic with an extrapolation coefficient; the teacher is an explicit model.
- Logit-space extrapolation (φ=logits / next-token distributions): extrapolate at the output distribution level (implemented via a geometric mixture / distributional extrapolation), producing token-level targets without necessarily materializing a full parameter-space teacher.

Training alternates RLVR and OPD in a recursive loop: RLVR grounds the direction (so extrapolation is not amplifying arbitrary drift), and OPD distills the extrapolated teacher into the student via token-level KL/CE. Key design knobs are β, anchor lag, and the choice of φ, each trading off compute, stability, and how “local” the teacher remains to the student.89:T526,An end-to-end pipeline:
- Web-graph construction: represent a web corpus as a directed hyperlink graph; improve out-link recall by merging a semantic mirror (RDF triples) with rendered markup.
- Task synthesis: sample an answer-anchored seed page, expand to a local subgraph, distill noisy pages into a connected entity graph, then generate a multi-hop question over that graph.
- Anchor removal / entity rewriting: abstract away directly searchable anchors so the task requires evidence composition across hops rather than single-query lookup.
- Dual-criteria verification: keep only tasks that are both sufficiently difficult and objectively checkable.
- Trajectory collection + filtering: roll out a strong teacher, then apply multi-stage filtering at both trajectory and turn levels to remove low-signal steps (irrelevant browsing, broken evidence chains, hallucinated citations).
- Training: start with filtered SFT; then do RL against live web search with an in-cluster judge and an observation summarizer; use iterative “SFT–RL climbing” where successful RL rollouts are fed back into the next SFT round to stabilize learning and improve sample efficiency.

OPD supervises the student on trajectories sampled from the current student policy, matching the student distribution to the teacher distribution along student-generated prefixes. The paper starts from the sequence-level reverse KL and uses its exact token-level decomposition. In practice, the main implementation is student top-k OPD: at each step, compute the KL only over the k tokens with highest student probability, after renormalizing both student and teacher on that subset. This choice is practical: much cheaper than full-vocabulary KL, but denser than sampled-token supervision.

The main contribution is not a new pipeline architecture but the rejection-outcome decomposition. Instead of counting rejections or final accuracy alone, the paper tracks what each rejection actually did: fix a wrong answer, damage a correct one, fail because the executor ignored the critique, or induce a wrong correction. This decomposition exposes two common evaluation mistakes. High rejection rate does not imply useful review, and low observed damage does not imply reviewer quality if the executor simply refuses to follow bad critiques. In other words, reviewer quality and critique uptake are separate variables and must be analyzed separately.8e:T69e,The headline result is straightforward. The fixed executor solves 52 out of 100 Olympiad math problems correctly. Replacing no-review with a cross-family mid-tier reviewer raises final accuracy to 64%, a gain of 12 percentage points with p=0.0005, and with zero damaged correct answers. This shows that a reviewer does not need full task-solving ability to create net value if it can reject the right cases.

Self-review is the more revealing condition. It achieves the highest detection rate, yet yields no significant accuracy gain. The paper reports that self-review rejects about 2.1 times as often as the effective mid-tier reviewer, but repairs only about one-third as many answers. It also falsely rejects 35% of the executor’s correct answers. The crucial detail is what happens after those false rejections: whenever the executor actually follows the critique, the revised answer becomes wrong. Cases that appear harmless are harmless only because the executor ignored the critique. This is the empirical basis for the paper’s claim that apparent self-review safety is often revision inertia in disguise.

At the low end, the weak reviewer is effectively inert. It changes none of the 100 final answers while roughly doubling token cost. That gives a practical capability floor: below some threshold, review neither repairs errors nor triggers useful revisions, and only adds overhead.

The other is to reuse this decomposition for data filtering, reward-model pre-screening, or synthetic reasoning-trace auditing.90:T875,AgentBrew has three stages. First, it collects a one-shot raw trajectory corpus in the target environment. The agent explores the live state of the application, proposes grounded tasks, and executes them. Importantly, the collected trajectories are not filtered by quality. This design choice is central: in real applications, interaction is expensive and success rates are low, so discarding most trajectories is not viable.

Second, the framework performs retrospective task inference. Instead of treating the original instruction as the only valid label, it infers what the trajectory actually accomplished by looking at the action sequence, tool calls, state transitions, and final outcome. This produces an aligned instruction-trajectory pair. The motivation is clear: many trajectories fail at their original goal but still complete some related or partial task. If trained against the original instruction, they become mislabeled supervision; if discarded, they become wasted data. Retrospective inference repairs this mismatch by relabeling behavior according to realized effects.

Third, AgentBrew applies PMI-based credit assignment. The total information a trajectory provides about its inferred instruction is written as pointwise mutual information, and then decomposed into additive per-action contributions using the chain rule. Intuitively, an action receives high credit if it substantially increases the evidence that the inferred task has been accomplished, and low credit if it is redundant, ineffective, or off-target. These per-action credits are then used as sample weights during policy training, amplifying gradients from informative actions and suppressing noisy ones. This is a more data-efficient alternative to rejection sampling or trajectory-level filtering, because useful local behavior can be retained even inside globally unsuccessful trajectories.

Conceptually, the method sits between behavior cloning and offline RL. It does not optimize with online interaction, and it does not assume a reward model or verifier. Instead, it reconstructs latent task structure from raw logs and then performs weighted offline policy learning.91:T57d,The evaluation is conducted on three real MCP applications: GitHub, Notion, and PostgreSQL. These are live, stateful tool environments rather than simulators, which makes the setup more convincing than synthetic agent benchmarks. Against rejection sampling, it gains +5.9 accuracy and +10.3 score. That comparison is important: it suggests that better supervision extraction from the same raw data can matter more than scaling the base model.

A full careful read should take around 45–60 minutes.93:T514,The central idea is soft router anchoring: gently pull the router toward the base router’s routing tendencies during training, without freezing it.
- Router Prior Bias (RPB): a training-time logit bias that attracts router logits toward a prior read from the frozen base router, while leaving router parameters trainable.
- Retention is measured at three levels, with the bias hook removed at evaluation (bias-free measurement): (1) per-expert utilization, (2) token-level top-k expert selection overlap, and (3) expert co-activation community structure (measured via NMI on co-activation graphs).
- Empirical pattern: soft anchoring methods (RPB and several alternative objectives that constrain router parameters/probabilities) achieve better downstream performance and retain top-k/community structure, while re-applied LBL mainly preserves utilization.
- Causal separation via interventions: enforcing the same prior as a hard assignment preserves community structure as well or better but reduces performance; shuffling prior content at fixed soft enforcement (within-community shuffle) barely changes performance. This supports the claim that the gain comes from soft enforcement/training dynamics rather than community preservation per se (community retention is a footprint, not the cause).94:T521,The generation process is formulated as a token-level MDP. The state is the prompt plus the generated prefix, transitions are deterministic token appends, and the verifier reward is observed only at the terminal position. Under ordinary value regression on stale trajectories, the squared-loss minimizer follows the Bellman operator of μ, so repeated critic updates converge toward V^μ. The actor, however, needs advantages based on V^π. The induced bias is position dependent: it is largest near the beginning of a response because the remaining suffix is generated under the stale policy.

BRACE modifies the value target rather than only the actor objective. It uses a k-capped correction horizon, applying importance correction only over the next k policy tokens after each position. This avoids multiplying π/μ ratios over an entire long sequence. Beyond that local window, it attaches an anchored Monte Carlo tail with a constant weight, so the terminal reward still reaches every position. The design separates local policy-mismatch correction from long-range reward propagation. This is the key difference from V-trace: with a short V-trace window, the target may contain no terminal reward; with a full-length window, the product of clipped importance ratios becomes unstable over long trajectories.95:T6b4,The core method is still directional ablation, adapted to MoE, multi-stream residuals, and FP8 weights. The basic recipe is to estimate a refusal direction from a few hundred contrastive prompts, then orthogonalize the weights that write to the residual stream against that direction so the model can no longer express refusal along it. The technical difficulty comes from three shifts. First, in an MoE, the residual writers are no longer just attention and dense MLP projections; routed experts and shared projections also matter. The paper shows that if one reuses the old dense-model implementation based on module-name traversal, many fused expert parameters are never touched. The edit appears to run cleanly but changes almost nothing, which creates a silent-failure mode. Second, GLM-5.3-Flash uses a four-wide hyper-connection residual. The authors argue that this topology does not fundamentally block directional ablation because the stream-mixing weights are scalar: if a direction is zeroed in every stream, later mixing keeps it zero. This is why directly editing residual-writing weights is more complete than hooking layer outputs. Third, the paper tests whether the single-direction hypothesis survives at frontier scale. It does not rely only on rank-1 ablation; it also tries higher-rank fitted subspaces and uses random orthogonal directions as controls. The main technical conclusion is twofold: the editable part of refusal is distributed across attention, dense/shared projections, and routed experts, and a nontrivial residue remains even after low-rank subspace removal, concentrated in a few content categories.
